text:
B: Hiya.
A: Hello. I'm Prajakta.
B: Leanne. Sorry, can you say that again?
A: Prajakta. It's fine. People usually get it on the third go.
B: Prajakta. Right. Got it.
A: So. Are you at work? You've got a fleece with a logo.
B: No, I'm on lates. Start at two. I just haven't bothered getting changed.
A: What do you do?
B: Shift manager. Warehouse off the M62, distribution. I run the late shift, about forty of them. Pickers, loaders, couple of team leaders.
A: Forty people. That's a lot.
B: It is when half the agency don't turn up. Tuesday I had six ring in sick and three just never showed. So you're rejigging everybody, moving people off loading onto picks, and the pick rate's still got to be where it should be or I get it in the neck. D'you know what I mean.
A: Yes. I don't manage anyone. I wouldn't want to.
B: Mm.
A: I'm a QC analyst. Pharmaceutical manufacturing, in Stevenage. We test the raw materials and the batches before they're released. HPLC mostly, and dissolution testing.
B: No idea what them are.
A: It doesn't matter. It's checking the tablet has what it says in it, and that it dissolves properly. If it fails, it's out of specification, and then there's an investigation and a lot of paperwork.
B: Sounds stressful, that.
A: It is, sometimes. If something's gone wrong I think about it at night. Even when it wasn't my mistake.
B: Yeah. We've got audit in three weeks.
A: Internal or customer?
B: Customer. They come round with a clipboard, check your training records, your return-to-work forms. And mine are, erm. They're not all where they should be, let's put it that way.
A: You should do them now. Not the week before.
B: I know. Everyone says that.
A: Because it's right. We had an inspection last year. The people who left everything to the end were the ones who got findings.
B: Bloody hell. You sound like my ops manager.
A: Sorry. I just mean it's easier.
B: No, you're right. It's just boring. I'd rather be on the floor sorting stuff out than sat filling in forms.
A: I'm the opposite. I'd rather check the forms than run samples all day. That's what I want to move to, a reviewer role.
B: Each to their own. Do you do long days an' all?
A: Thirty-seven and a half, plus overtime when the batches back up. Then I come home, make dinner, do my daughter's spelling. I'm shattered by nine.
B: I'm not even home till gone twelve. I have me tea at like half one in the morning.
A: Tea at half one?
B: Dinner, whatever. Air fryer chips usually. Dog sat there watching me.
A: That doesn't sound very healthy.
B: It's not. Don't tell me mam.
